verses.text: As Jesus was walking along, he saw a man who had been blind from birth.
His disciples asked him, “Rabbi, who sinned—this man or his parents—that he was born blind?”
Jesus answered, “It wasn’t that this man sinned, or that his parents did. This happened so God’s work could be shown in him.
While it’s still day, we must do the work of the One who sent me. Night is coming, when nobody can work.
As long as I’m in the world, I am the light of the world.”
After saying this, Jesus spat on the ground, made mud with the saliva, and spread it over the man’s eyes.
Then he told him, “Go wash in the pool of Siloam” (which means “Sent”). The man went, washed, and came back able to see. 👁️
His neighbors and the people who had seen him begging before started asking, “Isn’t this the man who used to sit and beg?”
Some said, “That’s him.” Others said, “No, he just looks like him.” But the man kept saying, “I’m the one.”
So they asked him, “How did your eyes get opened?”
He answered, “The man called Jesus made mud, spread it on my eyes, and told me, ‘Go to Siloam and wash.’ I went, washed, and now I can see.”
They asked him, “Where is he?” He said, “I don’t know.”
They brought the man who had been blind to the Pharisees.
The day Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes was the Sabbath.
So the Pharisees asked him again how he had received his sight. He told them, “He put mud on my eyes. I washed, and now I see.”
Some Pharisees said, “This man can’t be from God; he doesn’t keep the Sabbath.” Others said, “How could a sinner do signs like these?” They couldn’t agree.
So they asked the man again, “What do you say about him? He opened your eyes.” He said, “He’s a prophet.”
The Jewish authorities still refused to believe that he had been blind and had received his sight. So they called his parents
and asked them, “Is this your son, the one you say was born blind? How can he see now?”
His parents answered, “We know this is our son, and we know he was born blind.
But we don’t know how he can see now, or who opened his eyes. He’s old enough to answer for himself. Ask him.”
His parents said this because they were afraid of the Jewish authorities. The authorities had already agreed that anyone who confessed Jesus as the Messiah would be kicked out of the synagogue.
That’s why his parents said, “He’s old enough. Ask him.”
So they called the man who had been blind in again and said, “Give glory to God. We know this man is a sinner.”
He answered, “I don’t know whether he’s a sinner. Here’s what I do know: I was blind, and now I can see.”
They asked him again, “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?”
He replied, “I already told you, and you didn’t listen. Why do you want to hear it again? You want to become his disciples too?”
They insulted him: “You’re his disciple. We’re Moses’ disciples.
We know God spoke to Moses. But we don’t even know where this man comes from.”
The man answered, “Now that is wild! You don’t know where he comes from, yet he opened my eyes.
We know God doesn’t listen to sinners. But if someone worships God and does what he wants, God listens to that person.
From the beginning of the world, nobody has ever heard of anyone opening the eyes of someone born blind.
If this man weren’t from God, he couldn’t do anything.”
They shot back, “You were born steeped in sin, and now you’re trying to teach us?” Then they threw him out.
Jesus heard they had thrown the man out. When he found him, he asked, “Do you believe in the Son of God?”
The man answered, “Who is he, sir? Tell me, so I can believe in him.”
Jesus said, “You’ve seen him. He’s the one speaking with you now.”
The man said, “Lord, I believe!” Then he worshiped Jesus.
Jesus said, “I came into this world for judgment: so those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”
Some Pharisees who were there heard him and asked, “Are you saying we’re blind too?”
Jesus answered, “If you were blind, you wouldn’t be guilty of sin. But you say, ‘We see,’ so your sin remains.”
